clue.text: Wait for convict to finish sentence

indicators.note: the convict comes at the end, finishing the sentence word

parts.note: a prison sentence is time, as in 'doing time'
an old lag is a convict

explanation.surface: A prisoner waits for his term to run out.
explanation.definitionFit: A lag of time is an interval of waiting between cause and effect.

clue.text: It's the end of the line for Virgil, that's the long and the short of it

definitions.text: It's the end of the line for Virgil
definitions.meaning: the final foot of a Latin hexameter line, as written by Virgil, may be a long syllable followed by a short one

definitions.text: the long and the short of it
definitions.meaning: taken literally, a metrical foot made of one stressed or long syllable then one short

explanation.surface: A remark about how Virgil ends his lines, summed up in a cliché.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody this foot is a long syllable then a short one, and it can close a dactylic hexameter line.

clue.text: The regiment of Kipling's 'giddy harumfrodite?

definitions.meaning: the ... Regiment was a British Army infantry regiment named after the old county next to London
Kipling's soldier-and-sailor marine is a 'giddy harumfrodite', a hermaphrodite, which is jokingly a person of an in-between gender

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking which regiment Kipling's comic marine belonged to.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem 'Soldier an' Sailor Too' calls the marine a 'giddy harumfrodite'; split the answer as MIDDLE SEX for that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermaphrodite is jocularly of an intermediate gender, and Middlesex was also an English county regiment.

clue.text: True love found in ally, perhaps

indicators.note: the love letter is found inside the rearranged ally letters
perhaps signals that the word ally is only one possible ordering of its letters

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Genuine affection turns up in a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges ALLY to LYAL; 'found in' puts O inside it after the first L.
explanation.definitionFit: A true friend is a faithful, steadfast one.

clue.text: No-nonsense Dickensian whose class didn't finish hard task

indicators.note: the class word stops before its last letter

parts.note: a grade is a class or rank
a grind is laborious, tedious work

explanation.surface: A stern Victorian schoolmaster whose pupils never completed a gruelling assignment.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gradgrind of Hard Times wants 'nothing but facts'. 'didn't finish' cuts GRADE to GRAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Thomas Gradgrind is the fact-obsessed utilitarian schoolmaster of Hard Times.

clue.text: Exaggeratedly playing eccentric part in Turandot

parts.note: in engineering an eccentric is a cam, an off-centre wheel on a rotating shaft
Ping is one of the three ministers, Ping, Pang and Pong, in Puccini's opera Turandot

explanation.surface: An actor hamming up an odd role in Puccini's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like an adjective about the playing, but it is the noun: a mechanical cam.
explanation.definitionFit: Camping it up is acting in an affected, overdone, theatrical way.

clue.text: Name outstanding players, once you are able

indicators.note: read as the name standing out among the players, placed within them

parts.note: the cast of a play are its players

explanation.surface: A request to list the star performers, if you can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks an archaic form: thou canst means you can.
explanation.definitionFit: Canst is the old second-person singular of can, used with thou, meaning have the ability.

clue.text: For cheese, put out Parmesan without an alternative

indicators.note: an alternative arrangement of the remaining letters is wanted

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the cheese name is given without the two letters spelled a-n

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook told to leave out Parmesan with no substitute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes AN from PARMESAN, leaving PARMES; 'alternative' rearranges OUT + PARMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is slang for cheap, ordinary cheese such as bland Cheddar, fit only for baiting traps.

clue.text: Certain customers conceal a tiny hearing-aid

indicators.note: the two words conceal a run of letters across their join

explanation.surface: Some shoppers hide a small hearing device.
explanation.definitionFit: The incus or anvil is a tiny bone of the middle ear that helps transmit sound.

clue.text: French estuary eroding in storms

indicators.note: storms toss the letters of eroding about

explanation.surface: A river mouth in France is worn away by bad weather.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gironde is the estuary in south-west France where the Garonne and Dordogne meet.

clue.text: How curiously to get fed from field?

definitions.meaning: in a strange or curious manner
take the first, third and fifth letters of field, the odd-numbered positions, and they spell fed

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how grazing animals feed from a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a letter trick: the odd-placed letters of FIELD are F, E, D.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means strangely, and also by odd-numbered positions, as in picking alternate letters.

clue.text: News-reader taking exceptional care about new name

indicators.note: the rearranged care wraps around the other letters
exceptional care is care out of the ordinary, rearranged

parts.note: a noun is a naming word in grammar

explanation.surface: A broadcaster takes unusual care over a new name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'name' is not a person's name here but the grammatical naming word.
explanation.definitionFit: On radio or television the person reading the bulletins is a presenter of the news.

clue.text: Almost stop running away in the gloom

indicators.note: almost all of the word, missing its final letter

parts.note: halt means stop
flight is escape, running away

explanation.surface: Someone nearly halts while fleeing in the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims HALT to HAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim twilight, neither full day nor dark, is a dusky dimness.

clue.text: Member of communal sect taken short in German city

indicators.note: the sect member's name is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: the Essenes were an ancient Jewish sect living communally

explanation.surface: A member of an ancient sect gets caught short in a city in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr region of Germany.

clue.text: Doctor's exercises-the alternative way to salts, for example

indicators.note: the other way round, read from right to left

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor, so doctor's gives MO'S
PE is physical education, exercises

explanation.surface: A medic's exercise regime as an alternative route to health salts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the alternative way' turns MOSPE into the town name; 'to' links it as the word that goes with salts.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom salts, magnesium sulphate, take their name from the Surrey town with its mineral spring.

clue.text: Dives, getting marks perhaps on trousers

indicators.note: in a down clue the money sits on top of the trousers

parts.note: German marks are an example of money
bags are loose trousers, as in Oxford bags

explanation.surface: A diver ends up with marks on their trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives is the rich man in the parable of Lazarus, not a plunge into water.
explanation.definitionFit: Dives, the Latin for rich man, names the wealthy man of the parable, a person with lots of cash.

clue.text: Attacking in writing

parts.note: taken as written
cursive is joined-up handwriting

explanation.surface: A two-word puzzle: how can writing be an assault?
explanation.definitionFit: An incursive force makes raids into territory, so it is invading or aggressive.

clue.text: Moss or fern in cellar covering old inscription

indicators.note: in a down clue the cellar word sits above and covers the inscription

parts.note: a crypt is an underground chamber or cellar
ogam, or ogham, is an ancient Celtic alphabet carved on stones

explanation.surface: Moss grows over an ancient carving in a vault.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptogam is a plant reproducing by spores rather than seeds, such as mosses and ferns.

clue.text: Not giving any mess — it is clean

indicators.note: any mess made of the words it is clean jumbles their letters

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to allow any mess, insisting it is clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'any mess' rearranges IT IS CLEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inelastic does not stretch or yield under pressure.

clue.text: When in winter to put on gloves?

definitions.text: When in winter to put on gloves?

parts.words: When in winter to put on gloves?
parts.note: reads as a question about cold hands, but means the day for a boxing match, putting on boxing gloves, a British holiday on 26 December

explanation.definitionFit: The 26 December holiday falls in winter and its name suggests pugilists donning gloves.

clue.text: Plant showing insect damage

parts.note: a bug is an insect
loss is harm or damage suffered

explanation.surface: A plant shows signs of being attacked by pests.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugloss is a bristly plant of the borage family.

clue.text: Ploughman say with cheddar finally included in pub snacks

indicators.note: the letter is included inside the snacks

parts.note: pies are typical pub snacks

indicators.note: finally means the final letter of cheddar

explanation.surface: A ploughman's lunch with cheddar as part of bar food.
explanation.walkthrough: Piers Plowman is the hero of Langland's medieval poem; the surface wants a ploughman's lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Piers is the name of the ploughman in the medieval poem Piers Plowman, so an example of one.

clue.text: Guide has no right to travel excessively

indicators.note: the guide word has no letter for right in it

parts.note: to steer is to guide
to ply is to travel regularly back and forth

explanation.surface: A tour guide with no rights travels far too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has no right' removes R from STEER, leaving STEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Steeply, as in prices rising steeply, means sharply or to an excessive degree.

clue.text: Toothless and swollen, man clutches medal

indicators.note: the man holds the medal letters inside him

parts.note: a guy is a man
MM is the Military Medal

explanation.surface: A battered old soldier, toothless and puffy, holds tight to his medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swollen' is part of the definition, not a container signal; the Military Medal is a British gallantry award.
explanation.definitionFit: A gummy smile shows gums but no teeth, and a gummy ankle is puffy or swollen.

clue.text: A tiny piece before middle of Mattins as an anthem

indicators.note: the speck comes before the next letter

parts.note: a mote is a speck, a tiny particle

indicators.note: the central letter of the seven-letter word Mattins

explanation.surface: A short composition comes before the midpoint of morning service as its anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: Mattins is morning prayer in the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short sacred choral composition, much like a church anthem.

clue.text: Affected to display numbers in fashionable sequence

parts.note: hit means affected, as in hard hit
to parade is to display or show off

explanation.surface: Someone pretentious showing off their figures in trendy order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' looks like pretentious; here it means struck.
explanation.definitionFit: The charts list popular songs, musical numbers, ranked by how much in vogue they are.

clue.text: Jacob was not dangerous

definitions.meaning: in Genesis Jacob was smooth-skinned while his brother Esau was covered in hair
risky or frightening, in informal use

explanation.surface: A claim that the biblical Jacob posed no threat.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau was the shaggy twin, Jacob the smooth one; informally the word also means perilous.

clue.text: A service sent up for tea producer

indicators.note: in a down clue sent up means written bottom to top

parts.note: Mass is a church service

explanation.surface: A service sends a message up to the tea grower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent up' turns MASS to SSAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Assam, in north-east India, is a major tea-growing region.

clue.text: Removed top covering — it's disconcerting

parts.note: out means removed or taken away
a facing is an outer covering layer

explanation.surface: Someone stripped of their outer layer finds it unsettling.
explanation.definitionFit: Outfacing someone means staring them down, unnerving them with boldness.

clue.text: Arrange to be leading at tennis?

definitions.meaning: a player ahead by a set is a set in front

explanation.surface: Fixing things so you are ahead in a tennis match.
explanation.definitionFit: Set up means organise; read as set up, it is one set ahead in tennis.

clue.text: Meet say it's wrong to eat fox's head

indicators.note: the jumbled letters swallow the fox letter
the words say it's are put wrong, jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the head of fox's is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone claims it is wrong to eat a fox's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in the fodder carries no letter; the jumble gives SATISY, which the fox's F enters.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet a need or demand is to fulfil it.

clue.text: Call on operatic heroine to offer sincere flattery

indicators.note: the call is placed on, after, the heroine

parts.note: Mimi is the heroine of Puccini's La Bohème
to cry is to call out

explanation.surface: A request to a soprano to praise someone honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: From the saying 'imitation is the sincerest form of flattery'.
explanation.definitionFit: Copying someone, the proverb says, is the sincerest form of praise.
